answer.label: Not Eleanor Roosevelt — origin unknown (anonymous saying)
answer.authorDates: First documented 1978 · a floating inspirational saying
answer.sourceLine: Quotation researchers Ralph Keyes, Fred R. Shapiro and Barry Popik found no substantive link to Eleanor Roosevelt, and archivists have not been able to locate it in her writings. The earliest known print appearance is a 1978 classified ad in The Surrey Leader (British Columbia) — anonymous, and only pinned to Roosevelt from about 1986.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: The future belongs to those who have the courage to believe in the beauty of their dreams.
source.trailTitle: How an anonymous line became a Roosevelt quote
trail: 1978 — earliest documented print: a classified ad in The Surrey Leader, Surrey, B.C., reading ‘have the courage to believe in the beauty of their dreams’ — no author named (Quote Investigator ↗).
1983 — a Chula Vista newspaper reviewing graduation cards credits the line to ‘Thomas Mallory’ (likely a garble of Sir Thomas Malory) — not Roosevelt (Quote Investigator ↗).
c. 1986–1988 — the Eleanor Roosevelt attribution appears, in Gerson G. Eisenberg’s Learning Vacations and then Ms. magazine (Quote Investigator ↗).
Present — Wikiquote lists it under Roosevelt’s ‘Disputed’ section, noting it cannot be found in her writings (Wikiquote ↗).
source.cutTag: ↑ the 1978 version includes ‘have the courage to’ — later trimmed
source.excerptNote: The earliest strong match, a 1978 newspaper classified ad, carries the longer wording ‘have the courage to believe’; the streamlined form now attributed to Eleanor Roosevelt appears later and anonymously.

author.name: Unknown (anonymous saying)
author.heading: So who actually said it?
author.bio: This is a floating inspirational aphorism with no established author. Its earliest documented appearance is a 1978 classified advertisement in a British Columbia newspaper, where it ran without attribution. Over the 1980s it was variously credited to a ‘Thomas Mallory’ and, by about 1986, to Eleanor Roosevelt — but no primary source ties it to her or to any named writer.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely mis-credited ‘inspirational’ lines on the internet — printed on cards, posters and graduation banners under Eleanor Roosevelt’s name, with no source behind it.

items.why: Three leading quotation researchers — Ralph Keyes, Fred R. Shapiro and Barry Popik — found no substantive link, and archivists have not been able to locate the line in her writings. The Roosevelt tag first appears around 1986, decades after her 1962 death (Quote Investigator ↗).

A 1983 Chula Vista newspaper reviewing graduation cards credited the saying to ‘Thomas Mallory’ — probably a garbled reference to the 15th-century Le Morte d’Arthur author — another sign the line was circulating without a settled author (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the saying is anonymous. Its earliest documented use is a 1978 classified ad, and no evidence connects it to Eleanor Roosevelt (Wikiquote — Disputed ↗).

context.heading: Why the Roosevelt name stuck
lead: Eleanor Roosevelt is a magnet for orphan quotations. As a beloved humanitarian who genuinely wrote reams of accessible, uplifting prose — her ‘My Day’ column ran for decades — she is a plausible-sounding home for almost any earnest line about courage, fear or dreams. That plausibility is exactly what lets a misattribution spread.

Here the mechanics are visible in the record: an anonymous saying circulating in newspaper ads and greeting cards through the late 1970s and early 1980s, then hardening into a ‘Roosevelt quote’ once a 1986 travel guide and a 1988 magazine printed it under her name. From there, quote sites copied one another until the attribution looked authoritative.
context.detailsSummary: The thematic near-miss in Roosevelt’s real writing
detailsBody: Roosevelt did write about dreams — for example, a 4 July 1957 ‘My Day’ column reflecting that people ‘tried to bring their dreams of liberty to reality.’ The theme overlaps, but the wording is entirely different, and such passages are not the source of the aphorism; they simply make the false attribution feel right to readers.
context.pull: An anonymous card sentiment became a ‘Roosevelt quote’ simply because someone, somewhere, printed her name under it.
